The platform establishes three major monitoring subsystems-blasting vibration, concrete temperature and equipment localisation-and utilises the Cesium engine to load oblique photogrammetry models and spatially annotate measurement points. abstract: The electrical power industry is entering a period of unprecedented growth, with U.S. demand projected to rise at rates two to six times higher than historical trends, driven by data centers, electric vehicles, and the electrification of industrial, commercial, and residential systems. This acceleration is exposing the limits of legacy protection and control (PAC) design tools, which have remained largely unchanged for more than two decades. Electrical power system design projects are reaching record levels, even as workforce losses outpace new hires, forcing PAC engineers and designers to deliver more with fewer personnel. To meet future design challenges, PAC engineers and designers should consider evaluating, adopting, and implementing next-generation intelligent platforms that enable data-driven workflows, enhanced automation, and integrated digital twins. This paper outlines key considerations for modernizing PAC design processes, including evaluation and implementation timelines, pilot project strategies, staff onboarding, template development, 3D modeling, technical support, change management, and integration with enterprise systems. Furthermore, the paper examines how modern design tools can be integrated into broader IT infrastructures such as enterprise resource planning (ERP) and product data management (PDM) systems, panel manufacturing equipment, digital substation design, and other design platforms to create a more connected and automated engineering process. This paper highlights how intelligent tools can deliver results such as single line and threeline schematics, wiring diagrams, wire numbering, error checking, bill of materials (and other report) generation, and integrated smart objects in a centralized database. Smart objects let designers reuse devices from a database across a project, keeping the device connected through a database rather than placing disjointed graphic symbols. The paper also addresses legacy data challenges and proposes strategies for phased migration into new platforms. Finally, a look into what features could be enhanced in the future with the assistance of AI will be examined.

abstract: This research addresses the significant challenges of infrastructure construction in complex plateau environments by developing an intelligent monitoring system implemented in the cargo terminal project of Kunming Changshui International Airport. This study provides a scalable intelligent management solution for engineering construction in challenging environments, with its core innovation lying in the collaborative data fusion mechanism that enables proactive risk prevention and control. To address the need for safety monitoring in complex underground environments, this study puts forward a digital twin. construction method for underground prefabricated structures based on steel sheet piles. The method integrates finite element analysis, proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), and machine learning techniques to establish a scaled cantilever steel plate model. By combining load identification with reduced-order modeling, it enables real-time prediction and visualization of structural stress and deformation. The system facilitates dynamic monitoring, load inversion, and safety warning during the construction process. Maintains high computational while significantly reducing computational cost and data latency, thereby providing a feasible pathway toward intelligent and resilient construction of underground prefabricated structures.

title: Building An Elastic, Resilient, Scalable Cloud-Native Digital Twin by Leveraging Stream Adaptation Agents for Smart Distributed Manufacturing Systems
authors: Kedar P.; Mulpuri V.
abstract: Industrial digital twins operating across geographically distributed manufacturing facilities must simultaneously contend with concept drift, workload surges, and infrastructure failures conditions that expose a fundamental gap in static, periodically retrained architectures: they treat adaptation, resource provisioning, and resilience as independent, offline concerns rather than as jointly managed operational properties. This paper addresses that gap with a cloud-native systems architecture that closes the adaptation-provisioning-resilience control loop in a single, continuously operating coordination plane. The architecture integrates four tightly coupled infrastructure mechanisms: stream-resident Stream Adaptation Agents (SAA) that perform partition-level drift monitoring and quorum-gated orchestration; a Shared Adaptive Inference Layer that maintains a streaming ensemble model updated in-place without service interruption. The implementation runs on Apache Kafka, containerized services on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) on Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and cross-provider replicated checkpoints on GCP and Amazon Web Services (AWS). Evaluations use production-inspired industrial telemetry workloads across six operational scenarios. Against established streaming drift detectors and infrastructure baselines: stream-native SAA orchestration recovers predictive accuracy to 0.93 in 145 steps versus 601 steps for periodic full retraining and permanent degradation to 0.77 for a static model; the adaptation-aware workload score W(t) = αλ(t) + βA(t) eliminates SLA violations where fixed-replica provisioning produces 8.14%; cross-provider active-passive failover achieves 98.8% availability versus 90.0% single-cloud, an 8.3× reduction in mean downtime; SAA orchestration overhead is 0.013 ms/step at eight agents, confirming edge co-deployment feasibility. © 2026 IEEE.

abstract: In order to handle the growing energy demand, water scarcity, waste production, and environmental sustainability issues, smart cities need intelligent resource management. But current resource management frameworks generally optimize resource use in each infrastructure separately, reducing the ability of coordinated decision making among interacting urban services. To overcome this, this study introduces a Digital Twin Assisted AI Framework (DTAI-RM) for smart city resource management for sustainability. It combines hierarchical digital twin, multi-modal IoT data fusion, demand forecasting with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and a Twin-Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) algorithm, to facilitate cross-domain optimization of energy, water, waste, and building resources adaptively. A reward mechanism that is aware about sustainability further optimizes the use of resources by considering energy efficiency, operational cost, water conservation and carbon emission. The proposed framework is assessed with a city scale digital twin in relation to multiple urban infrastructures operating under realistic operating conditions. The results of the experiments show significant gains compared to the conventional approaches in energy efficiency (91.37%), water-loss reduction (88.54%), waste collection optimization (84.92%), reduction in operational costs (86.73%) and reduction in carbon emissions (83.68%). These findings illustrate the potential of using AI-powered digital twins in conjunction with predictive analytics and reinforcement learning to optimize the coordination of resources, increase operational resilience, and reduce environmental impact. The proposed DTAI-RM framework aims to be a scalable, intelligent and sustainable tool for next generation smart city resource management. © 2026 IEEE.

abstract: Sim-to-real transfer remains a key challenge for the effective deployment of autonomous agents, as mismatches in perception, vehicle dynamics, and actuation can significantly degrade performance. We propose a low-cost, fully reproducible pipeline where a 1:10-scale Traxxas Slash vehicle serves as the physical twin of a model in the CARLA simulator, both operating under the same continuous action space. On the real platform, an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano executes the control policy and interfaces with an Arduino Due for sensor acquisition and PWM-based actuation. The digital twin is validated on a parking maneuver by executing the same reference policy in both domains and comparing yaw, lateral acceleration, and lateral offset using Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) and Maximum Normalized Cross-Correlation (MNCC). Results confirm high-fidelity reproduction of the real platform dynamics. Building on this validation, a PPO reinforcement learning agent is trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot on the physical vehicle. The policy achieves comparable performance, with only minor degradation primarily due to ultrasonic perception noise rather than dynamic mismatch. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study demonstrating effective zero-shot transfer of a purely-simulation-trained autonomous scale vehicle.

title: CIM Wizard: A Flexible Framework for Automated CityJSON Generation from Sparse Urban Data
authors: Taherdoustmohammadi A.; Schiera D.S.; Patti E.; Bottaccioli L.; Mazzarino P.R.

abstract: Urban Energy Modelling (UEM) bottom-up approaches involve three phases: data modelling, model extraction, and simulation. The tight coupling of these phases in existing tools limits flexibility and reuse. CIM Wizard addresses the data modelling phase through a pipeline of independent, interchangeable calculators that transform sparse urban datasets into standardised City Information Models (CIMs), while deliberately leaving model extraction and simulation to interoperable downstream tools. Users add new enrichment methods by defining a calculator class and a single JSON configuration entry, with no framework-level changes required. A priority-based fallback mechanism handles missing data, while a topological dependency resolver guarantees correct execution order. Resulting CIMs are stored in a PostGIS spatial database and exported as CityJSON extended with Energy and Utility Application Domain Extensions (ADEs). A real-world Italian case study demonstrates that fragmented municipal data can be transformed into detailed CIMs suitable for urban planning, scenario analysis, and digital twin applications. © 2026 IEEE.

authors: S. Mihai; M. Yaqoob; D. V. Hung; W. Davis; P. Towakel; M. Raza; M. Karamanoglu; B. Barn; D. Shetve; R. V. Prasad; H. Venkataraman; R. Trestian; H. X. Nguyen
abstract: Digital Twin (DT) is an emerging technology surrounded by many promises, and potentials to reshape the future of industries and society overall. A DT is a system-of-systems which goes far beyond the traditional computer-based simulations and analysis. It is a replication of all the elements, processes, dynamics, and firmware of a physical system into a digital counterpart. The two systems (physical and digital) exist side by side, sharing all the inputs and operations using real-time data communications and information transfer. With the incorporation of Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), 3D models, next generation mobile communications (5G/6G), Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), distributed computing, Transfer Learning (TL), and electronic sensors, the digital/virtual counterpart of the real-world system is able to provide seamless monitoring, analysis, evaluation and predictions. The DT offers a platform for the testing and analysing of complex systems, which would be impossible in traditional simulations and modular evaluations. However, the development of this technology faces many challenges including the complexities in effective communication and data accumulation, data unavailability to train Machine Learning (ML) models, lack of processing power to support high fidelity twins, the high need for interdisciplinary collaboration, and the absence of standardized development methodologies and validation measures. Being in the early stages of development, DTs lack sufficient documentation. In this context, this survey paper aims to cover the important aspects in realization of the technology. The key enabling technologies, challenges and prospects of DTs are highlighted. The paper provides a deep insight into the technology, lists design goals and objectives, highlights design challenges and limitations across industries, discusses research and commercial developments, provides its applications and use cases, offers case studies in industry, infrastructure and healthcare, lists main service providers and stakeholders, and covers developments to date, as well as viable research dimensions for future developments in DTs.

By designing a five-layer architecture comprising sense, store, model, view and application layers, the platform overcomes key technical challenges such as multi-source heterogeneous data fusion, lightweight three-dimensional modeling, and real-time visualization, achieving high-fidelity dynamic mapping between the physical campus and digital space. The platform employs a layered decoupling system consisting of data foundation, middle platform, and governance applications, establishing a unified governance data resource center that facilitates cross-departmental data sharing and business collaboration. Practical applications demonstrate that this platform effectively promotes the transition of university management from traditional approaches to a data-driven modern governance model, providing a feasible technological pathway for smart campus development. Distinct from existing solutions that focus on isolated 3D visualization, this work's core contribution lies in its holistic, practice-proven architecture that integrates a reusable data middle platform with a scalable cloud-rendering 3D engine, validated through quantifiable improvements in governance efficiency and resource optimization in the university.

Four thematic clusters have emerged: design for sustainability, digital innovation (e.g., BIM, IoT), circular economy for materials, and equitable governance. The professionalism of China, the UK, and the USA is clearly in the lead, while there is far less research in the area of informal settlements, and the context of the Global South is generally disadvantaged. This is the only bibliometric review that considers post-2020 innovations in urban housing and sustainability construction as its own analysis. This study represents a methodological innovation in considering Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and MetaAnalyses (PRISMA)-informed screening.” The analysis offers a new mapping opportunity to view the evolution of the field and highlights gaps related to equity and resilience.

title: A BIM-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Human–Robot Collaborative Construction with On-Site Scanning and Adaptive Path Planning
authors: M. Yuan; H. Mao; W. Qin; B. Wang
source_title: 2025 5th International Conference on Computer Vision, Application and Algorithm (CVAA)
abstract: As the Architecture 4.0 paradigm advances, integrating robotic systems into construction workflows has become vital to address labor shortages and enhance execution precision. However, conventional BIM-based automation struggles to cope with dynamic, cluttered on-site environments. This study presents a closed-loop digital twin framework that fuses 3D BIM modeling, real-time sensor-based site scanning, and human-robot interaction to enable adaptive collaboration in architectural construction. The system continuously updates its digital twin using LiDAR and RGB-D DATA to capture spatial deviations, unexpected obstacles, and environmental changes. Based on these inputs, the robot’s motion trajectories are recalculated through an online path replanning module. We validate the system using a wall panel dry-hanging case, involving a 6 degrees of freedom (6 DoF) ABB robotic arm and a Unity-VR interface for immersive human supervision. Across 24 experimental runs in cluttered environments, the adaptive system achieved a $92.4 \%$ average placement accuracy, reducing positioning error by $47 \%$ compared to static BIM-based workflows. Obstacle avoidance success rate reached $\mathbf{9 5. 8 \%}$, and average task completion time decreased by $18.6 \%$ due to reduced manual intervention. These results demonstrate the framework’s potential to transition construction robotics from pre-scripted automation to intelligent, real-time collaboration.

abstract: Automatic methods for reconstructing buildings from airborne Lidar point clouds focus on producing accurate 3D models in a fast and scalable manner, but they overlook the problem of delivering simple and regularized models to practitioners. As a result, output meshes often suffer from connectivity approximations around corners with either the presence of multiple vertices and tiny facets, or the necessity to break the planarity constraint on roof sections and facade components. We propose a 2D planimetric arrangement-based framework to address this problem. The two key ideas are first to regularize, not the 3D planes as commonly done in the literature, but a 2D polyhedral partition constructed from the planes, and second, to extrude this partition to 3D by an optimization process that guarantees the planarity of the roof sections as well as the preservation of the vertical discontinuities and horizontal rooftop edges. We show the benefits of our approach against existing methods by producing simpler 3D models while offering a similar fidelity and efficiency. © 2024 IEEE.

authors: Xue N.; Liang Z.; Zhang Z.; Jin L.; Wang J.

abstract: Smart buildings and the Internet of Things (IoT) are driving a growing need for accurate indoor positioning to support services such as facility management, digital twins, and human-machine interaction. Radio-frequency systems like Wi-Fi and UWB are common, but their accuracy is often limited by bandwidth rules and multipath effects. Visible-light positioning (VLP), which reuses existing LED lights, avoids radio interference and keeps costs low. However, its received-signal-strength (RSS) and the fingerprints data can be disturbed by obstacles and noise, so single-model solutions are less likely to reach a higher accuracy. We introduce a low-complexity two-stage VLP method that first uses an improved multilayer perceptron (MLP) network for a 1st-stage positioning estimate, then refines it with a 2nd-stage upgraded k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) searching method. Measurements show that the average errors of the plain KNN and plain MLP are 11.54 cm and 8.44 cm, which are reduced to 8.70 cm and 7.53 cm after the algorithm improvements; their fusion further lowers the mean error to 6.62 cm. The approach runs in milliseconds and needs no extra hardware, offering an easy, low-cost path to high-precision indoor VLP.  © 2025 IEEE.

Recent studies address this problem using geospatial information, three-dimensional urban representations, line-of-sight analysis, blind-zone reasoning, and occlusion-aware modeling. However, the literature remains fragmented across transportation sensing, wireless network planning, and infrastructure-based perception. abstract: Digital Twin technology is vital for making informed decisions during the maintenance of built assets. It is important for the information in the Digital Twin to be as accurate and up-to-date as possible. To maintain the accuracy of the Digital Twin, the data on the building’s geometric parameters must be regularly updated. abstract: Industry 4.0 (I4.0) is accompanied by a variety of technologies which offer great potential for optimizing the manufacturing of electric motors. However, the application of I4.0 technologies in this sector has hardly been examined yet. For determining I4.0 potentials in the electric motor production, a structured approach is required since the variety of sub-processes and production technologies results in a vast number of possible combinations. Therefore, this paper first compares different generic approaches for identifying, selecting and implementing I4.0 use cases. Building on this, a methodical approach is derived in order to tap the numerous I4.0 potentials within the electric motor production. On the one hand, use cases can be derived from current technological opportunities resulting from application examples and best practices in research and industry. On the other hand, concrete problems in critical manufacturing processes can give rise to the application of novel I4.0 solutions. By presenting a comprehensive overview of promising application scenarios, this paper mainly facilitates the identification of I4.0 potentials in the electric motor production from an opportunity-driven perspective. In addition to approaches directly addressing the electric motor production, concepts can be derived from related processes in other application domains. Examples are provided by outlining a selection of the presumably most relevant use cases. The results indicate that especially data-driven approaches, i.e. data analytics and machine learning, offer great potential in electric motor production. As an outlook, I4.0 potentials can also be disclosed from a problem-pull perspective, supplementing the opportunity-push approach of this paper. © 2018 IEEE.

abstract: Educational innovation is a daily challenge for both students and teachers. Over the years, new pedagogies and models have been developed so that both stakeholders can make the most of the spaces inside and outside the classroom. In response to this, there are various tools that not only facilitate student engagement in the class but also enable the instructor to use them to make sessions more active and raise the cognitive level. An example of what was described above is virtual or digital laboratories; these are interactive platforms that adapt to different styles of learning and teaching. In addition to this, they promote collaboration among students, motivate, nurture creativity, and allow for the repetition of experiences without the need to be physically present where the work is being done. This, in turn, results in the introduction of hybrid learning methods [1]. On the other hand, a tool that aids in the performance of these laboratories is photogrammetry, which is a remote information capture system. It includes remote sensing and photointerpretation, techniques that complement each other. However, it can be affirmed that photogrammetry is realized through a quantitative interpretation of aerial photographs and other aerial photographic materials to obtain maps [2]. The digitization of historical and urban buildings through photogrammetry has become an innovative tool for transforming the way students interact with the built environment and cultural heritage. This combination of technology and education enables students to actively explore and learn about urban heritage, thereby contributing to its preservation. With the previous paragraphs as context, the aim of this article is to demonstrate the effectiveness of using photogrammetry to create digital twins of buildings and thus transform the concept of digital laboratories. abstract: This paper presents the results of implementing innovative strategies using drones and 3D scanners in the specialization course Efficiency and Digitalization of Construction, aimed at undergraduate students of civil engineering and architecture. The course is offered as a specialization option among three alternatives in the penultimate semester of undergraduate programs in these fields: Sustainable Use of Water, Real Estate Intelligence, and Efficiency and Digitalization of Construction. In 2024, the course was attended by a group of 25 students from various campuses across the country. For the module on Structural Damage and Inspection Techniques, students engaged in traditional visual inspection activities of the campus stadium, identifying and qualitatively assessing damages using conventional management systems to evaluate damage severity. In contrast, a parallel activity was designed to implement advanced technologies, including 3D scanning with LiDAR and drones equipped with high-definition cameras, to identify and map damages. This technological approach enabled a quantitative and highly precise evaluation of damage severity through image analysis. When comparing these instructional strategies, incorporating technology and innovation into the cited module, students expressed, through end-of-course surveys, high motivation toward developing and researching technological solutions. They also recognized the importance of integrating high-precision technology into the evaluation and diagnosis of existing infrastructure. At the conclusion of the course activities, students and faculty prepared and submitted a technical report to campus administrators, detailing their findings and results. This report is expected to contribute to future maintenance and conservation projects, thus closing the cycle of specialization activities by observing the execution of physical interventions on the inspected stadium. Faculty members plan to continue these activities with the next cohort in the following academic year, allowing for the monitoring of damage progression and ensuring continuity in learning outcomes.

abstract: Aerial digital photogrammetry offers a viable alternative to traditional surveying, providing higher accuracy, lower operational costs, and a non-destructive approach ideal for mapping heritage sites. UAV's successfully capture 3D models of structures, accurately reproducing complex geometries at various resolutions. Our research presents a structured methodology for accurate 3D representation, involving the precision alignment of UAV imagery, GNSS RTK positioning for Ground Control Points (GCP's), and independent verification using a total station. From the aligned images, we generate dense point clouds, create orthophotographs, and vectorise facade surfaces into formats suitable for architectural analysis. The resulting metric measurements provide sufficient detail for precise architectural analysis, restoration planning, and long-term digital preservation. Beyond restoration, the georeferenced 3D model serves as a foundational building block for Virtual Reality (VR) applications and Digital Twins of heritage sites. These models allow users to evaluate cultural assets in unprecedented detail, interact with them innovatively, and simulate structural changes caused by natural or man-made disasters. Ultimately, aerial digital photogrammetry is a key component in creating a framework for the digital documentation and preservation of architectural heritage. This methodology opens numerous possibilities for multidisciplinary growth, particularly in developing immersive 3D models and visualizing them through virtual reality. © 2026 IEEE.

abstract: The digital transformation of construction value chains must drive the development and integration of innovative components and systems in the future built environment. This would support the transition from today resource-intensive practices towards a smart and regenerative circular economy, addressing increasing regulatory complexity and customized end-user requirements. Still its implementation faces challenges to enhance interaction and co-creation among stakeholders and to manage growing data volumes over the lifespan of construction products and buildings without unduly burden innovation stakeholders and especially SMEs. This article presents an exploratory case study of a digital clustering service based platform to help the European construction value-chains and their SMEs dealing with innovation development: clustering enhances knowledge sharing, opportunity matchmaking, and collaboration across the innovation lifecycle, facilitated by a digital platform providing access to value-added services. Two services are introduced as lighthouse examples: the Digital Product Passport, mandated by EU legislation to improve product traceability and transparency in support of the circular economy; and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation architecture based on a Large Language Model toolkit to accelerate document processing and navigation of complex construction regulations. This digital transformation case study, based on field tests and early observations, aims at assessing, from a managerial perspective, coordination of expertise and innovation leadership by value chains and SMEs. It stresses the role of systematic access to evolving regulations for better informed decision-making aligned with circular economy objectives. The main expected impact for construction SMEs is a transition from a ‘Business-as-usual’ innovation creation toward a co-development process by all holistic value-chain stakeholders over the innovation life-cycle stages, based on Innovation 2.0 principles and powered by a clustering platform.

abstract: A quiet but consequential transformation is reshaping North America’s digital infrastructure: Bitcoin mining farms are increasingly being repurposed into artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. As cryptocurrency mining profitability wanes and demand for AI compute surges, Bitcoin miners—already equipped with grid-connected power and large-scale digital infrastructure assets—offer AI companies a fast-track alternative to the time- and capital-intensive process of building new facilities. This article articulates the forces accelerating this trend, the technical and operational requirements for conversion, and the broader implications for power systems. We examine the key differences between Bitcoin mining and AI workloads, the evolving business models enabling this transition, and the impacts on grid stability, markets, and decarbonization. We highlight the importance of considering operational and embodied emissions in evaluating the sustainability of the transition from Bitcoin mining to AI data centers. Ownership of data centers also influences the environmental impact of operations, with hyperscale high-performance computing (HPC) data centers being owned by large tech companies with greater obligations to reduce emissions.

authors: E. Al-Tayar; S. A. Al-Azazi; A. Ali; A. M. Alawag

abstract: This paper develops a BIM-integrated, explainable, and deployment-aware decision-support framework for real-time personal protective equipment (PPE) monitoring in Yemen’s construction sector. Its contribution is an integration-based decision-support artifact rather than a new PPE detection algorithm. The study addresses a persistent practical gap: many vision-based PPE systems can detect violations, yet they rarely convert image-level detections into auditable, location-aware, and managerially defensible interventions. The assessment remains analytical, and field validation is left for future work. abstract: This paper examines the integration of Virtual Reality (VR) technology into Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for engineering projects. Traditional EIA methods often rely on written reports and static 2D visuals, which can limit stakeholder comprehension and reduce engagement. As engineering projects grow in complexity, these limitations hinder transparent decision-making and weaken the communication of ecological consequences. VR offers an immersive and interactive medium to visualize environmental impacts in three-dimensional space, enabling stakeholders to directly experience projected outcomes. By combining VR with advanced simulation platforms such as Integrated Environmental Solutions – Virtual Environment (IES VE), this study demonstrates how EIA can be enhanced to improve clarity, accessibility, and participation. Findings indicate that VR not only enriches assessment practices but also promotes more sustainable engineering outcomes by bridging the gap between technical analysis and public understanding. This integration of VR and simulation tools represents a step toward more inclusive, transparent, and effective environmental assessment.

This can act as a barrier for the submission of feedback and thus cause the facility management to remain unaware of unsatisfactory comfort conditions or faults, which can result in further issues and costs. This information is integrated and represented with semantic technologies, which allow to formally organize the information and describe the relationships between the data. title: Extracting and Formalizing Domain Knowledge from Legacy Infrastructure Data Through MBSE
authors: J. Gross; S. Eschlberger; K. Polanec; E. Bader; C. Neureiter
source_title: 2026 IEEE 31st International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA)
abstract: AECO still struggles to carry meaningful information across the lifecycle of an asset. Despite the use of BIM, IFC, and related digital workflows, critical knowledge is still fragmented across documents, software environments, and project phases, which makes it difficult to preserve semantics, trace decisions, and reuse information in later lifecycle stages. This problem is particularly pronounced for long-lived and safety-critical assets such as tunnels, where condition data, responsibility, and historical context must remain understandable over decades. To address this gap, the paper develops a modelbased systems engineering-oriented process for extracting and formalizing domain knowledge from legacy documents. The method structures heterogeneous information through five abstraction levels—Domain, Process, Artifact, Information Object, and Attribute—and iteratively refines it through decomposition, structuring, and selection. Applied to a large tunnel maintenance report, the process transforms defect-related information into a formal meta-model that is evaluated against requirements for scalability, interpretability, traceability, reusability, and readability. The results suggest that MBSE can serve as a strong backbone for turning legacy AECO information into structured, lifecycle-oriented knowledge. Rather than treating documents as static deliverables, the approach turns them into a persistent and actionable basis for a single point of truth.

title: Engineering a 2.5D Urban Twin: Semantic GeoAI Discovery and Blockchain-Provenanced Updates
authors: Nicula A.-S.
source_title: 2026 International Conference on Frontiers of Engineering and Emerging Technologies, FET 2026
abstract: This work presents an urban digital twin for Timioara, Romania built from fragmented public datasets in the absence of official 3D city models. The implementation integrates municipal CKAN resources, OpenStreetMap extracts, and Copernicus elevation data through adapter-based ingestion with enforced schemas and automated versioning. Three technical challenges motivated the design: heterogeneous coordinate reference systems (Stereo 70, WGS84, UTM Zone 34N) requiring canonical reprojection, conflicting update cadences across daily OSM snapshots and static municipal layers, and inconsistent geometry validity requiring automated repair workflows. Vector embeddings enable semantic search over dataset metadata; Precision@5 improves from 0.46 to 0.74 compared to keyword approaches, with P95 query latency under 510ms. Blockchain Merkle roots anchor data provenance while keeping geospatial files off-chain; tamper detection achieved 100% accuracy across 400 deliberate corruption trials. Ten repeated builds achieved identical hashes with 98.5% resource retrieval success, completing in 46 minutes with 2.8% cryptographic overhead. The system generates a 2.5D representation pairing OSM building footprints with inferred heights from Copernicus DEM and building-level attributes. The results demonstrate that operational urban twins can be assembled from incomplete, multi-authority sources when paired with strict version control, semantic discovery, and cryptographic integrity verification, enabling municipal stakeholders to query integrated infrastructure data reliably. © 2026 IEEE.

abstract: The convergence of digital twin (DT) technology and artificial intelligence (AI) represents a transformative advancement in sustainable infrastructure management. Through systematic review of 70 peer-reviewed publications spanning 2020 to 2026, key technological enablers including IoT sensor networks, machine learning algorithms, and edge computing platforms were identified. A taxonomic classification distinguishes data-driven approaches (60 percent) from physics-informed methods (17 percent) and hybrid implementations (23 percent), while architectural analysis compares centralized cloud-based systems with distributed edge computing deployments. The analysis reveals that AI-enhanced digital twins achieve energy optimization of 20 to 30 percent, predictive maintenance accuracy of 96 percent, and material recovery rates of 60 percent in circular economy applications. We propose a Sustainable Digital Twin Framework (SDTF) with detailed operational specifications for data acquisition, AI-based processing, decision support, and feedback control layers. Implementation challenges including data interoperability, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and formal verification requirements are analyzed alongside emerging solutions. Research limitations and future directions are identified to guide continued advancement. © 2026 IEEE.

source_title: Proceedings - Frontiers in Education Conference, FIE
abstract: The advancement of digital technologies is radically transforming the ways in which historical and architectural heritage is studied, preserved and passed on to future generations. This work proposes an integrated methodology for the digital reconstruction and management of historical monuments, based on the integrated use of Heritage Building Information Modeling (HBIM), Digital Twin (DT), IoT sensors and Machine Learning (ML) algorithms. Through the creation of high-fidelity digital models, updated in real time through environmental monitoring systems, it is possible to obtain a dynamic and predictive vision of the state of health of historical structures. The case study of the Leproso Bridge in Benevento, constitutes a concrete example of the application of this methodology: starting from surveys performed with terrestrial laser scanners and drone photogrammetry, an HBIM model was generated and subsequently integrated with data from environmental sensors, to develop a functional DT for the simulation of evolutionary scenarios, both historical and future. This digital platform makes it possible to visualise the transformations undergone by the artefact over time, monitor its current state, and predict structural degradation phenomena through automated analyses. In addition to its contribution in terms of conservation, the proposed approach represents an innovative educational resource. Students and teachers are involved in immersive, interdisciplinary learning experiences that combine art history, structural engineering, digital modelling and materials science. The interactive and data-driven environment fosters the development of transversal skills such as critical thinking, collaboration between disciplines and the conscious use of technology in heritage conservation. In conclusion, the combination of HBIM, DT, IoT and AI emerges as a powerful tool for both research and conservation design, as well as for historical memory education in a sustainable and participatory perspective © 2025 IEEE.

abstract: This Research to Practice Full Paper describes a project that combines different fields to include Heritage Building Information Modelling (HBIM), Internet of Things (IoT) sensor systems, and the digital twin (DT) concept into the hands-on learning experiences for construction engineering and architecture students at the university. This methodology was used in the 'Computer Graphics' course at the University of Salerno, where third-year students engaged in a data-driven digital workflow concerning the genuine case study of Villa Regina, a Roman rural villa situated inside the archaeological site of Pompeii. abstract: Longer space missions need autonomous systems that can sustain stable and secure living conditions inside confined habitats. This study presents an adaptive environmental management system using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), a reinforcement learning (RL) method, to control temperature, humidity, $\text{CO}_{2}$ concentrations, and air pressure. An advanced simulation environment was created to train the PPO agent, including authentic sensor functionalities and actuator limitations. The findings indicate that PPO enables intelligent, self-optimising environmental management with improved flexibility and energy efficiency. The proposed technology provides a scalable solution for life support in extraterrestrial habitats, establishing a crucial basis for viable expeditions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

abstract: To tackle challenges such as limited network bandwidth, scarce edge computing resources, and high virtual-real interaction latency in engineering Digital Twin (DT) systems at construction sites, this paper proposes a cloud-edge collaborative visual-semantic processing mechanism. First, a collaborative computing architecture of "lightweight extraction at the edge, global mapping in the cloud" is constructed. At the edge, an improved LE-YOLO network is designed, which reconstructs the backbone with GhostNet modules and integrates the CBAM attention mechanism. On NVIDIA Jetson Nano devices, the network achieves real-time inference at 38.5 FPS while maintaining an mAP of 83.5%, reducing parameters by 34.4% compared with YOLOv8n. Second, a structured JSON-based semantic streaming protocol is designed to enable efficient edge–cloud communication. Based on this protocol, a visual–geometric fusion mapping algorithm is further proposed, in which a ray-casting strategy is employed to map 2D visual semantics onto 3D BIM models in real time, achieving accurate virtual–real spatial alignment. Experiments show that this mechanism saves 99.2% of bandwidth compared to traditional video streaming under weak network conditions, eliminates congestion and stuttering caused by video backhaul, and controls end-to-end latency within 100 ms, effectively enabling low-latency and high-consistency virtual–real synchronization for real-world construction site perception tasks.

title: Physics Informed Neural Operator for Battery Health Prediction and Lifecycle Management
authors: Shivali; M. Manu; V. Saxena; G. S. Rawat; A. Jain; A. Goel

abstract: To achieve safe, reliable and cost-effective lithium-ion battery operation, it is important to predict accurately the lithium-ion battery state of health (SOH) and the remaining useful life (RUL). Nonlinear electrochemical aging processes control battery degradation, and pure data-based models finds difficult to make accurate long-horizon predictions, whereas physics-based models can be computationally demanding and hard to tune across operating conditions. In this study, a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) architecture is introduced to predict battery health and lifecycle. This approach trains the operator mapping between battery utilisation history and SOH trajectories with a Fourier Neural Operator backbone and adds physical constraints that ensure monotonic capacity dissipation, charge throughput consistency, and end of life that are physically realistic. The validation is done using public run-to-failure battery data, and SOH is defined as $\text{SOH} = \mathrm{C} \_$ now/C_0, which is a popular formulation in battery health research. abstract: The construction sector has come up against some serious challenges for years, including inadequate production efficiency, enormous safety hazards, and a huge waste of resources on site. Existing research often concentrates solely on individual technologies and does not systematically integrate these technologies into a comprehensive solution, which limits the application of technology for the real-time monitoring and precise control of complex construction sites through traditional manual inspection processes. In contrast to this past research, the present research is based on the integration of digital twin, building information modelling, computer vision and IoT technologies to create an intelligent construction site monitoring system for building engineering, which enables a complete view of the construction site, and provides intelligent identification and precise controls over the entire site. This research is being conducted through the use of a four-layer structure that includes a “perception-transmission-platform-application” system. The first layer includes the “perception” elements, which consists of the collection of information from multiple sources using ultra-wideband positioning base stations, trained multi-media equipment (e.g. high-definition cameras), environmental sensors and drones; transmission of collected information is executed through a 5 G edge gateway; intelligent processing of the collected data is performed using YOLOv8 networks, SlowFast behaviour recognition networks, DeepLabV3+ semantic segmentation networks, with the use of Kalman filtering to combine the images and perception data; and, finally, the completed data is used at the application layer for visualized monitoring of the construction site, three levels of intelligent early warning detect, and 4D process management. In data fusion, the root mean square error of personnel positioning is reduced to 0.35 meters, the tower crane status recognition accuracy is 91.3 %, and the false negative rate for abnormal events is 4.6 %. The resulting transparent decisionsupport system provides a quantifiable instrument to balance technological innovation potential, institutional effectiveness, and social equity; methodologically, the contribution lies in integrating dynamic game models with blockchain-enabled transparent governance, offering new quantitative support for technologyinstitution coordination.

abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach for indoor mobile robot navigation, focusing on environments like Ambient Assisted Living spaces (AAL), smart homes, and factories, where humans and robots coexist. The need for effective space and traffic management in these areas is critical for ensuring safety and mobility. Our novel Semantic Path Planning algorithm improves upon traditional grid mapping by using a multi-dimensional array in the map file, where varying intensities indicate occupancy levels. The planner imposes penalties on free cells near specific static objects based on user preferences, facilitating autonomous robot movement in designated areas without creating rigid barriers. A standout feature of our algorithm is its ability to prioritize specific zones frequented by vulnerable groups like the elderly, or areas designated for rest, pets, or children's play. By enhancing the A* path planner with semantic and geometric data, our approach enables the management of these zones, leading to a comprehensive grid map for optimal path-finding. Moreover, this methodology is promising for multi-robot systems with differing navigation abilities and access rights. It also improves robot localization by focusing on unique environmental landmarks, thereby enhancing tracking accuracy and aiding in swift localization recovery. This approach is ideal for safe, efficient, and context-aware navigation in dynamic shared human-robot environments.

authors: Ja'Far N.A.; Alauthman M.; Al-Jokhadar A.; Maqusi A.A.

abstract: Progress toward Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 11 depends on planning processes that connect building-level performance to city-level dynamics. Building Information Modelling (BIM) provides semantically rich, quantitative descriptions of assets, yet these models are commonly retained within project repositories and are not systematically used in municipal workflows. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and 3D city models contribute spatial context at urban scale, but they often lack the granularity required to evaluate embodied carbon, energy demand, accessibility, and resilience at the level of individual buildings. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-including graph learning, large language models, and neuro-symbolic approaches-make it increasingly feasible to integrate these sources and implement urban digital twins that can support policy formulation and design evaluation. This paper presents a governance-Aware conceptual framework that integrates BIM, GIS/CityGML, and urban sensing through a layered pipeline for data ingestion, semantic integration, AI analytics, and SDG-Aligned decision support. In lieu of a prototype, the paper reviews work reported during 2021-2025 and critically examines persistent barriers and emerging directions, including semantic interoperability, privacy-preserving data governance, generative urban design, and automated SDG compliance checking. Because data availability varies widely across cities, we also discuss data-readiness tiers and fallback strategies for contexts where BIM, IoT streams, or semantic 3D city models are incomplete, fragmented, or unavailable. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Digital Twins as an Integrative Platform for Energy Efficiency, Renewable Integration and Global Competitiveness of Energy Companies: A Conceptual Synthesis
authors: Ergunova O.; Skvortsova I.; Somov A.G.; Chayuk S.; Dusenko S.; Mukhanova G.
source_title: 2026 International Conference on Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics, and AI Applications, ICCSDFAI 2026
abstract: Digital twin (DT) technology is rapidly evolving from isolated engineering models into an integrative platform linking building energy performance, renewable generation, grid operation and corporate competitiveness of energy companies. Research remains weakly interconnected across three streams: building-level energy simulation, renewableenergy systems and managerial perspectives on digital twins as a strategic asset. This paper presents a conceptual synthesis based on a focused review of seven recent peer-reviewed sources (2023-2026), positioned against classical DT scholarship and current standardisation efforts (ISO 23247, IEC 63278, the Asset Administration Shell). We propose a three-layer integrative framework - Asset Layer, System Layer and Strategic Layer - that maps DT functionalities onto energy efficiency, renewable integration and competitive positioning of energy firms. The framework is operationalised through two illustrative quantitative cases: a 10,000 square metre office building, with annual savings of about 300 MWh, a simple payback of about 7.5 years and a positive net present value at an 8 percent discount rate over a 15-year horizon, and a 100 MW renewable plant, where curtailment is reduced by 3.5 percentage points, recovering about 7 GWh per year. To formalise the central finding, we introduce a Value-Capture Gap (VCG) metric and a composite Digital TwinCompetitiveness Index (DTCI). The synthesis suggests that the strategic layer remains underdeveloped relative to the asset and system layers, producing a measurable VCG between technological capability and business outcomes. Five crosscutting enablers are identified and a research agenda is outlined for closing the gap between digital-twin engineering and competitive strategy in the energy sector. © 2026 IEEE.

The RT simulation results based on 3D EM reconstruction closely align with channel measurement data, demonstrating higher accuracy than the 3D building model.

title: Hybrid-Grained Feature Aggregation with Coarse-to-Fine Language Guidance for Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation
authors: W. Zhang; H. Liu; B. Li; J. He; Z. Qi; Y. Wang; S. Zhao; X. Yu; W. Zeng; X. Jin
source_title: 2025 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
abstract: Current self-supervised monocular depth estimation (MDE) approaches encounter performance limitations due to insufficient semantic-spatial knowledge extraction. To address this challenge, we propose Hybrid-depth, a novel framework that systematically integrates foundation models (e.g., CLIP and DINO) to extract visual priors and acquire sufficient contextual information for MDE. Our approach introduces a coarse-to-fine progressive learning framework: 1) Firstly, we aggregate multi-grained features from CLIP (global semantics) and DINO (local spatial details) under contrastive language guidance. A proxy task comparing close-distant image patches is designed to enforce depthaware feature alignment using text prompts; 2) Next, building on the coarse features, we integrate camera pose information and pixel-wise language alignment to refine depth predictions. This module seamlessly integrates with existing self-supervised MDE pipelines (e.g., Monodepth2, ManyDepth) as a plug-and-play depth encoder, enhancing continuous depth estimation. By aggregating CLIP's semantic context and DINO's spatial details through language guidance, our method effectively addresses feature granularity mismatches. Extensive experiments on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms SOTA methods across all metrics, which also indeed benefits downstream tasks like BEV perception. Code is available at https://github.com/Zhangwenyao1/Hybrid-depth.

title: Ambiguity Subspace Resolution for Digital Twin Parameter Estimation
authors: W. Zirwas; B. V. Boas; L. Thiele
source_title: 2023 IEEE International Conference on Communications Workshops (ICC Workshops)
abstract: In this work, we analyze the limits of parameter estimation of multipath components like their amplitude, delay and/or phase. Especially challenging is the estimation of such parameters when the multipath components have a low relative delay, i.e., less than half a tap delay with respect to the discrete channel impulse response. We will introduce the concept of the ambiguity subspace, which indicates that even for high signal to noise ratios and quite large RF bandwidths the Fischer information is limited and accurate estimation of the real world parameters becomes challenging. To overcome these theoretical limits, we propose the idea of ambiguity subspace resolution, ideally providing a solution close to the correct parameter values. There are a number of applications, which may benefit from the knowledge of the real world parameters like positioning, or, channel prediction. Here, we have in mind the building vector data map describing the environment of a digital twin of a mobile network, which is inferred from regular UE feedback of radio channel estimates. Such a digital twin is expected to support 6G use cases from optimized beam management, handover, load balancing up to channel estimation and/or channel prediction.

abstract: Efficient irrigation infrastructure management is essential for achieving sustainable water distribution and agricultural productivity. Performance evaluation demonstrated efficient rendering and data loading, validating the system’s capability to handle high-fidelity BIM models in lightweight web environments. abstract: This paper presents the development of a Digital Twin framework for establishing a unified cadastral reference system in Indonesia. The research addresses persistent issues in the national cadastre, including data gaps, overlaps, and inconsistencies across institutions that arise from fragmented survey campaigns, heterogeneous mapping standards, and the absence of a unified, three-dimensional cadastral reference system capable of reconciling multi-agency datasets. At the international level, most existing Digital Twin implementations focus on infrastructure, mobility, or generic 3D city models rather than legally binding cadastre, leaving a gap in national-scale cadastral digital twins particularly in developing-country contexts. title: A Multi-Sensor LiDAR–Photogrammetry Workflow for 3D Documentation of Sumbawa Besar Heritage Sites Toward H-BIM Development
authors: T. Satriawansyah; L. Mulyadi; A. U. Krismanto; L. K. D. Erlinda; K. T. Suhari
source_title: 2025 1st International Conference on Data Science and Geoinformatics (ICDSG)
abstract: High-fidelity 3D documentation of historic wooden architecture is essential for cultural heritage preservation and the development of Heritage Building Information Modeling (H-BIM). This study presents a multisensor Li-DAR–photogrammetry workflow applied to three major heritage sites in Sumbawa Besar: Bala Datu Ranga, Istana Dalam Loka, and Istana Bala Puti. Each monument was captured using tailored sensor configurations adapted to architectural scale, interior complexity, and accessibility, with accuracy validated through device-generated quality assessments. For Bala Datu Ranga, a hybrid GNSS–LiDAR–Visual SLAM system was used in PPK mode supported by terrestrial ground control points. The resulting point cloud achieved 100% compliance with the 5 cm precision threshold. More than 80% of the points fall within the 1–2 cm error range, and residuals on ground control points were on the order of 3–6 mm, demonstrating high geometric stability across both indoor and outdoor areas. For Istana Dalam Loka, a combination of static terrestrial laser scanning and handheld SLAM-based scanning was employed. Registration produced a global alignment error of 0.003 m, with individual cloud-to-cloud link errors ranging from 0.001 m to 0.007 m and overlap levels between 23% and 83%. These results confirm strong consistency between scanning positions throughout the building’s expansive multi-level wooden structure. For Istana Bala Puti, rapid indoor–outdoor mapping using a mobile LiDAR–SLAM platform yielded 100% of points within the 5 cm threshold. Approximately 24.5% of the points lie within 0–1 cm, 47.8% within 1–2 cm, and 27.7% within 2– 5 cm, indicating accuracy sufficient for architectural modeling and heritage-scale H-BIM development. Trajectory stability and GNSS quality metrics further demonstrate reliable performance in GNSS-degraded conditions through fused visual–LiDAR SLAM. In summary, the multisensor fusion of static TLS, handheld SLAM, PPK georeferencing, and photogrammetric texturing produced dense and accurate point clouds suitable for semantic segmentation, structural interpretation, and H-BIM generation. The results demonstrate that integrating multiple sensor modalities significantly enhances completeness, minimizes occlusions, and accelerates data acquisition for complex wooden heritage architecture.

title: Implementation of a Digital Twin Framework in the Modular Housing Industry

abstract: The construction industry is one of the minor digitized industries, and it has been characterized by a below- average increase in productivity in recent decades. The modular housing sector copies the production system of the manufacturing industry to meet these deficits, which makes it a perfect example for evaluating Industry 4.0 technologies. This paper explores the methodology and possibilities of implementing a digital twin of a modular housing production plant to optimize its production. The proposed approach based on a Digital Twin (DT) framework consists of three consecutive parts: (1) analyzing the production system by using the Lean tool of Value-Stream Mapping extended (x-VSM) towards Discrete-Event Simulation (DES) models, (2) collecting real- time data to track and trace the system's bottleneck by using Radio-Frequency Identification Devices (RFID) as a Tracking- and-Tracing system (TaT), and (3) optimizing it by using DES. Three scenarios to eliminate waste, increase throughput, and identify the best possible TaT implementation have been simulated. The results are a 64 % inventory reduction, a 20 % faster production lead time, and the finding of the critical part to be tracked using RFID. The resulting model has shown to be a valuable instrument for understanding the different process interdependencies. Moreover, it has been used as a support tool for middle management to assess the impact of different optimization approaches quantitatively. Overall, this paper shows the implications of combining DES and TaT systems towards a DT of a modular housing production plant.

abstract: Modern methods such as off-site construction, modular building, and robot-based manufacturing promise efficiency gains in the timber construction sector. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are employed to analyze sheathing represented as point clouds, and to associate them with BIM data from the design phase. title: Progressive Building Instance Segmentation on the Hessigheim 3D Photogrammetric Mesh Benchmark
authors: Zhou S.; Lu Y.
source_title: 2026 7th International Conference on Geology, Mapping and Remote Sensing, ICGMRS 2026
abstract: High-resolution triangular meshes generated from oblique aerial photogrammetry are increasingly used for 3D urban representation. While per-face semantic labels can now be obtained from established classifiers, these labels do not distinguish one building from another, a capability required by downstream tasks such as building-level energy simulation, LOD3 reconstruction, and digital-twin maintenance. Existing instance segmentation methods typically depend on deep learning and large annotated datasets. Most operate on point clouds rather than meshes, leaving mesh-native adjacency and surface-normal information unused. We investigate this problem on the Hessigheim 3D benchmark using all 18 validation tiles with 11-class semantic annotations, each carrying instance-level ground truth, covering 68 buildings in total. Building on a classical geometric pipeline of clustering, fixed-threshold region growing, and postprocessing, we propose two improvements: Progressive Region Growing (PRG), which replaces the fixed-threshold merge with a multi-round scheme under gradually relaxed normal-similarity and height-difference thresholds, and Boundary Regularisation (BR), which removes isolated noise, fills gaps via convex-hull analysis, and smooths instance boundaries. The combined pipeline raises the F1 score from 0.744 to 0.840, with precision improving from 0.618 to 0.841. Ablation experiments confirm that PRG and BR contribute complementary gains and that their combination outperforms either module in isolation. A texture-colour variant confirms that geometric cues dominate over radiometric ones on this dataset. The pipeline requires no training data and no GPU resources. © 2026 IEEE.

abstract: As cities grow, they have more problems with traffic jams and keeping an eye on their infrastructure. This is why smart city development needs intelligent urban management systems. This paper presents a deep learning framework intended to tackle two essential urban analytics challenges: forecasting traffic flow and segmenting building footprints. The first part of the framework uses a Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network (ST-GNN) to understand how traffic changes over time, using data from the METR-LA traffic speed dataset. The dataset is made up of many sensors that are spread out over road networks. Graph structures are used to show how the sensors are related to each other in space. The model combines multi-head graph attention mechanisms with gated temporal convolutional networks to effectively capture patterns in traffic data over time and space. The model predicts traffic conditions for the next 12 time steps using the Huber loss function. Its goal is to minimize the normalized Mean Absolute Error (MAE). The second part uses SpaceNet satellite images and an optimized U-Net architecture to segment building footprints. The encoder-decoder structure with skip connections lets classify pixels accurately while keeping spatial details and high-level semantic features. This method makes segmentation work better, even in tough urban settings like shadows, changing light, and dense building structures. All of these parts work together to make an integrated framework that supports AI-driven urban analysis. This helps with smart city planning, monitoring infrastructure, and developing digital twins. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Methods, Sectors, and Ways: Artificial Intelligence for Decision-Making in Urban Circular Economy Transitions (A Narrative Literature Review)
authors: Kinanda R.; Sutriadi R.; Wijaya N.
source_title: 2026 13th International Conference on ICT for Smart Society, ICISS 2026
abstract: The transition toward an urban circular economy (CE) is fundamentally a complex decision-making challenge characterized by highly heterogeneous data streams, fragmented policy landscapes, and conflicting stakeholder objectives. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a vital mechanism for data processing, existing research remains siloed within individual technical applications or localized sectors. To address this gap, this study conducts a narrative literature review with thematic synthesis to examine how AI comprehensively supports decision-making in urban CE transitions across three core dimensions: applied methodologies, operational sectors, and decision-making quality. The synthesis reveals a complementary division of labor where analytical methods (machine learning and predictive analytics) serve as cognitive engines, while physical systems (computer vision and AI-driven robotics) act as the operational executioners. Infrastructurally, AI interventions primarily stabilize the heavy-emission flows of the energy and waste management sectors, while emerging applications in the built environment, urban mobility, and bio-metabolic loops (water and agriculture) reshape spatial and resource circularity. Furthermore, this study establishes that AI elevates the caliber of governance from reactive crisis containment to an evidence-based, proactive paradigm. This is achieved by anchoring decisions in multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), predictive lifecycle design, and cyber-physical Digital Twins that automate regulatory compliance and simulate real-time scenario testing. Ultimately, this review offers a consolidated framework illustrating that successful urban circularity depends on integrating regional and urban planning with adaptive digital ecosystems, positioning intelligent decision support at the core of sustainable metropolitan governance. © 2026 IEEE.

title: Data Prediction and Abnormal Forewarning for Space Environment Simulator Based on Three-Layer Framework
authors: X. Su; W. Zhang; J. Liu; Z. Li; R. Deng; J. Hao; H. Long; Y. Zhang
source_title: 2021 7th Annual International Conference on Network and Information Systems for Computers (ICNISC)
abstract: During the operation of the key equipment of the space environment simulator, the equipment signals collected through sensors show non-stationary, small sample size and strong timing characteristics. The commonly used device health management methods are difficult to cope with such complex signals. To this end, a three-layer framework is proposed to achieve data prediction and abnormal forewarning for critical equipment in space environment simulators. The framework consists of a signal data segmentation layer, a data prediction layer, and an anomaly monitoring layer. The specific approach is to segment the signal sequences into sub-sequences using a sequence segmentation algorithm, and then identify each sub-sequence type using DNN. abstract: Digital twin technology supports intelligent management by linking physical assets to their virtual models. We present an edge-oriented visual perception system for these conditions. The system is organized around three main stages. First, a semantic-constrained image rectification module corrects perspective distortion and produces standardized cabinet views. Second, a panoramic reconstruction process stitches multiple close-range images into a complete cabinet view. title: Agentic AI in Optical Networks: Navigating the Autonomy and Abstraction Trade-offs
authors: M. Ahmadian; C. Natalino; P. Monti
source_title: 2026 26th International Conference on Transparent Optical Networks (ICTON)
abstract: Agentic AI systems — where large language models (LLMs) autonomously plan, reason, and act — are emerging as a compelling paradigm for managing the complexity of optical networks [1, 2]. Two independent design axes shape any such system. The first is autonomy: whether the LLM freely sequences tool calls and decides when to stop (ReAct-style open loop [3]), or whether control flow is pre-encoded as a deterministic graph, with the LLM invoked only at fixed decision points. The second is application programming interface (API) abstraction: whether the agent interacts with the network through semantic, domain-specific tools that encapsulate protocol details (high abstraction) or through raw protocol primitives that require the LLM to construct RESTCONF paths, resolve UUIDs, and parse nested YANG-model JSON directly (low abstraction). Note that high API abstraction reduces the LLM’s reasoning burden at the tool-call level, whereas low API abstraction demands greater in-context synthesis from the LLM — a distinction that is important when interpreting accuracy differences across LLM variants. Prior demonstrations over NETCONF/YANG [4] and OpenConfig [5] have shown the feasibility of LLM agents in optical network management, but none have characterized the architectural trade-offs that follow from these two choices. The gap matters: operators deploying agents on live infrastructure need to know which position in this design space best fits their requirements for generality, predictability, and trustworthiness. This paper makes two contributions. First, it establishes the autonomy × abstraction framework as basis for reasoning about agentic AI design choices in optical networking, covering all four quadrants of the design space. Second, it grounds the framework in three concrete implementations over the same T-API [6] digital twin: (i) a high-autonomy, high-abstraction ReAct agent with 18 domain-specific tools covering topology queries, optical performance monitoring (OPM), quality of transmission (QoT) analysis, and network (re)configuration across 12 scenarios; (ii) a low-autonomy, high-abstraction directed graph workflow that constrains the LLM to fixed invocations within a compiled agent graph with fully deterministic branching, including a modulation format cascade (DP-64QAM → DP-16QAM → DP-QPSK) executed without any LLM involvement; and (iii) a highautonomy, low-abstraction variant that replaces the 18 domain tools with 2 generic HTTP primitives, requiring the LLM to construct raw T-API RESTCONF paths, resolve UUID references, and navigate nested YANG-model JSON directly. The low-autonomy, low-abstraction quadrant — a directed graph calling raw protocol endpoints — exists conceptually but offers no practical advantage over the other three concrete implementations and is left as a boundary case. The three implementations are compared across five dimensions, three structural and two empirical. Generality: the high-autonomy ReAct agent handles all 12 scenario types covering topology queries, OPM, path analysis, lightpath provisioning, and multi-turn management; the directed graph handles lightpath provisioning only, evaluated across 100 randomly sampled node pairs from the CORONET CONUS topology. Predictability: every execution path of the directed graph is a deterministic function of typed state and fully enumerable at design time; the ReAct agents produce traces determined at inference time with unbounded tool-call sequences. Constraint enforcement: the directed graph embeds domain rules in branching logic the LLM never sees, enforced independently of model quality; both ReAct variants rely on the system prompt, making enforcement contingent on model compliance. Human oversight: the low-abstraction tools require the user to interpret low-level messages exchanged between the agent and the network controller, while the high-abstraction set of tools allow more precise human oversight due to each tool being linked to a specific functionality. Token cost: we measure how many tokens are necessary for each system realization to achieve a pre-defined set of goals as a representation of the cost to accomplish the tasks. Three key outcomes can be mentioned. High autonomy should be preferred when task diversity is high, and the full set of management scenarios cannot be anticipated at design time. Low autonomy should be preferred when predictability and auditability are safety requirements, or when domain constraints must be enforced independently of model behavior. On the abstraction axis, high API abstraction consistently reduces LLM error surface, prompt complexity, and operator evaluation burden; the engineering cost of building domain-specific tools is recovered in reliability and is progressively offset as interfaces such as T-API and model context protocol (MCP) standardize semantic operations at the protocol level.

abstract: The digitalization process is steadily increasing in the building industry and promises new perspectives for better designing and operating buildings throughout their life cycle. However, digitalization has not yet brought its greatest benefit for tackling the rising global energy demand and is even generally associated with more energy consumption. Instead, it has become urgent to rationalize energy use and decrease energy wastes. Indeed, buildings are responsible for about one third of the global energy consumption in the world [1], and 30% of this energy is even wasted through wrong or suboptimal operation, malfunctions and energy-unaware user behavior. Technologies supporting resource saving already exist for e.g. fault detection and mitigation, optimized energy systems control or predictive maintenance. But they necessitate much manual effort by experts to be configured and deployed since every building is to some extent unique with regard to its location, equipment and usage. Moreover, they require much expert knowledge and are not adapted for a daily usage by facility managers or even building users. These measures require also many data for continuous observation, analysis and system adaptations in real time. Although modern building management systems (BMS) can generate lots of monitoring data from sensors and meters, there is still poor or no reuse of building design data already produced in preliminary stages of the building life cycles. In view of these facts, this paper proposes a new data management workflow that relies on the reuse of building design information for facility management, and that shall fasten the deployment of energy-saving services while increasing user energy awareness and engagement in reducing energy use. For that purpose, this workflow makes use of building information modeling (BIM), knowledge graphs, data analysis and web technologies in order to develop a BIM-based Digital Twin for energy saving in the building operation phase. © 2023 IEEE.

abstract: Integrating real-time sensor data into Building Information Models (BIM) has been a game changer in the field of facility management and building energy optimization. BIM and real-time sensor data plays a crucial role in offering immediate insights that improve decision-making, enhance operational efficiency, increase safety measures, and optimize resource allocation. This paper presents a case study of Swinburne University's Advanced Technologies Centre (ATC) building for integration of live sensor data from Internet of Things (IOT) cloud using DFROBOT Firebeetle Espressif (ESP) 32 microcontroller and Dynamo visual programming. The results present a workflow for the real-time cloud-based data collection and storage of live sensor data with successful integration to BIM model. Further, a framework for visualizing the captured data in Virtual Reality (VR) environment has been proposed for enhanced facility management.

title: An Exploration of Metaverse Applications in the Health Sector and Their Limitations
authors: Y. Zafar
abstract: Since the COVID-19 pandemic an upsurge in technological innovation can be observed and this development is contributing to the building of the metaverse. In congruence with other aspects of life, the health sector has shifted its focus to provide alternatives to normal medical practice by introducing new applications powered by AI, VR, Machine Learning and advanced deep learning techniques to create technology that is accurate, versatile, safe and convenient. This study looks at how current AI powered tools have eased the process of identifying cancer, bone fracture detection, enhancing precision medicine and tele-medicine services. Other medical applications have been developed to assist in decision making processes, treatment planning and management of health institutions. Robot assisted surgeries and remote surgeries have seen vast improvement, namely the use of the Tianji robot and Micro Hand robot. This report further looks at the future scope of health applications in the metaverse, observing that information is distributed, and the human centered design, security and privacy concerns that are presenting challenges. It provides an up-to-date summary of the types of tools currently being used in the health sector and the studies that have been conducted to investigate their performance.

title: RoofSam: Adapting the Segment Anything Model to Rooftop Classification in Aerial Images
authors: A. Bauer; J. -C. Krabbe; K. Kollek; J. Velten; A. Kummert
source_title: 2024 58th Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems, and Computers
abstract: Foundation models, such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM), are transforming computer vision by enabling versatile architectures that can adapt to new tasks with minimal domain-specific data. In the geospatial context, however, these capabilities have been primarily examined for SAM's intended use case, image segmentation. This paper aims to extend SAM's capabilities beyond dense prediction by introducing RoofSAM, an adaptation of SAM specifically designed for roof shape classification in high-resolution aerial images guided by building outlines. RoofSAM utilizes SAM's interactive interface to effectively incorporate readily available prior knowledge about building locations through point-sampling processes. We evaluate several sampling strategies, including centroid and random sampling approaches, to determine their effectiveness in enhancing model accuracy. Our empirical and visual analyses demonstrate that RoofSAM can successfully transfer SAM's segmentation knowledge to the task of roof shape classification, achieving F1-scores of up to 86% for frequently represented classes, even with limited training data. These results underscore the versatility of vision foundation models in geospatial data processing applications.
